intent_label: Transactional — the user wants a number to put on an invoice or quote.
intro: Value added tax is charged on the price of most goods and services in the UK and every EU member state. The one thing people get wrong is the direction: adding VAT means multiplying the net price, while removing VAT means dividing the gross price by 1 plus the rate. Subtracting the percentage from the gross figure gives the wrong answer every time, and on a 1,000 invoice the error is around 33.

This calculator handles both directions, defaults to the standard rate for twelve countries, and lets you type any rate you need. It shows the VAT amount, the net figure and the gross figure together, so the two numbers you put on an invoice always add back up to the total you are charging.

faqs.q: How do I remove VAT from a price?
faqs.a: Divide the gross price by 1 plus the rate. At 20% VAT, 600 ÷ 1.2 = 500 net, so 100 of the 600 was VAT. Never subtract 20% from the gross figure — that removes 20% of the gross, not 20% of the net, and understates the tax.

faqs.q: What is the difference between VAT and US sales tax?
faqs.a: VAT is collected at every stage of the supply chain, with businesses reclaiming the VAT they paid on inputs, so it is ultimately a tax on the final consumer. US sales tax is collected once, at the point of sale, and rates vary by state and city rather than by product category.

faqs.q: Are these VAT rates current?
faqs.a: The preloaded rates match the standard rates published by national tax authorities at the time of the last review shown on this page. Rates change — for example reduced rates are frequently used as temporary policy tools — so confirm the current rate with your national authority before issuing an invoice.

faqs.q: Is VAT charged on delivery and shipping?
faqs.a: In the UK and most EU states, delivery is part of the taxable supply, so it is charged at the same rate as the goods. If an order mixes standard-rated and reduced-rated items, the delivery charge is normally apportioned in the same proportion.

faqs.q: Why does my invoice total not match my bank payment?
faqs.a: Common causes are rounding at line level versus invoice level, a different rate applied to shipping, or a reverse-charge note on a cross-border B2B invoice where VAT is accounted for by the buyer rather than charged by the seller.

disclaimer: VAT treatment depends on the nature of the supply and the jurisdictions involved; confirm with your accountant or tax authority.
editorial_note: Rates are preloaded as a convenience, not as tax advice. The calculator shows the arithmetic; the applicable rate is your responsibility.

intro: A percentage is just a fraction with a denominator of 100, but the phrase around it changes the arithmetic completely. 20% of 150 is 30. 30 as a percentage of 150 is 20%. A move from 150 to 180 is a 20% increase, while 180 back down to 150 is a 16.7% decrease. Each of these is a different question, which is why so many people reach for a calculator rather than risk the wrong formula.

This tool has four modes covering those cases, shows the formula it used, and includes the reverse case — working backwards from a final amount to the original — which is the one most people get wrong when removing a tax, a discount or a fee.

faqs.q: What is the difference between percentage change and percentage points?
faqs.a: Percentage points measure the simple difference between two percentages: a rate moving from 5% to 8% rises 3 percentage points. Percentage change measures that move relative to the starting value: the same jump is a 60% increase. News stories about interest rates usually mean percentage points.

faqs.q: How do I calculate a reverse percentage?
faqs.a: If you know the amount after a percentage has been added, divide by 1 plus the rate as a decimal. If it was removed, divide by 1 minus the rate. For 20% VAT, 600 becomes 500 because 600 ÷ 1.2 = 500.

faqs.q: Why do percentage increases and decreases not cancel out?
faqs.a: Because they apply to different bases. A 50% rise from 100 gives 150; a 50% fall from 150 gives 75. To return to the original value after a 50% rise you need a 33.3% fall.

faqs.q: Can percentages be negative?
faqs.a: Yes. A negative change simply means a decrease. This calculator shows the sign explicitly so a fall is never confused with a rise.

disclaimer: Results are exact arithmetic on the numbers you enter; they do not model rounding rules used in specific tax or exam systems.
editorial_note: Every mode prints its formula, because the formula is the part people actually need to learn.

faqs.q: How many working hours are in a year?
faqs.a: A 40-hour week over 52 weeks is 2,080 hours, which is the standard US figure. A 37.5-hour UK week gives 1,950. If you take unpaid holiday or unpaid breaks, subtract those hours — the calculator lets you set paid weeks per year for exactly this reason.

faqs.q: Is this a take-home pay calculator?
faqs.a: No. It converts gross pay between periods. Income tax, national insurance, social security and pension contributions depend on where you live and your personal situation, so applying a generic deduction would produce a misleading number. Use your employer's payroll or your national tax office calculator for net pay.

faqs.q: What does pro rata mean?
faqs.a: Pro rata means in proportion. A 30,000 full-time salary worked at 22.5 hours a week instead of 37.5 becomes 30,000 × (22.5 ÷ 37.5) = 18,000. Enter the part-time hours and the full-time salary to see the equivalent.

faqs.q: Should holiday be included in the hourly rate?
faqs.a: For employees, paid holiday is included in the salary, so use the weeks you are paid for, which is usually 52. For freelancers and contractors, holiday is unpaid, so use 46 to 48 working weeks to build a realistic day rate.

faqs.q: Why is my payslip hourly rate different from this figure?
faqs.a: Payroll often uses a fixed divisor, such as 2,080 hours or 26 fortnights, rather than your actual hours, and may include allowances or overtime in the base. Check which divisor your employer uses before comparing.

editorial_note: We deliberately do not estimate net pay: tax rules vary by country and household, and a generic deduction would be wrong for most visitors.

intent_label: Commercial investigation — the user is sizing a loan before committing, or checking an existing offer.
intro: An equated monthly instalment keeps the payment the same every month while the split between interest and principal shifts. Interest is charged on the outstanding balance, so in the early years most of each payment is interest; by the final years almost all of it is principal. That is why a 20-year loan at 9% costs almost twice its face value in interest, and why prepaying in year three saves far more than prepaying in year fifteen.

This calculator applies the standard reducing-balance formula, shows the full amortisation schedule, and compares your result against a scenario where you add a fixed extra amount to each payment, so you can see the interest saved and the months cut.

examples.title: 250,000 over 20 years at 9.5%
examples.body: The EMI is about 2,330 a month. Total repayment is about 559,300, so interest alone is roughly 309,300 — more than the amount borrowed. In the first year, interest accounts for about 92% of what you pay.

examples.title: The same loan with 200 extra each month
examples.body: Paying 200 more every month clears the balance around five years earlier and saves roughly 90,000 in interest. The earlier the extra payment starts, the larger the saving, because it attacks the balance that interest is charged on.

faqs.q: How is EMI calculated?
faqs.a: EMI = P × r × (1 + r)^n ÷ ((1 + r)^n − 1), where P is the principal, r is the monthly interest rate (annual rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100) and n is the number of monthly payments. The result stays constant while the split between interest and principal changes each month.

faqs.q: What is the difference between flat rate and reducing balance interest?
faqs.a: Flat rate charges interest on the original amount for the whole term, so a 10% flat rate on 100,000 over five years costs 50,000 in interest. Reducing balance charges interest only on what is still owed, so the same nominal 10% costs roughly 27,000. Always compare APRs, not headline rates.

faqs.q: Does prepaying a loan save interest?
faqs.a: Yes, and the saving is largest early in the term because the outstanding balance is highest. Check whether your lender charges a prepayment penalty and whether the loan uses reducing balance; on a flat-rate loan the saving is calculated differently.

faqs.q: Why is my bank's EMI slightly different?
faqs.a: Differences usually come from fees rolled into the principal, a different day-count convention, rounding to the nearest rupee, pound or euro each month, or an insurance product added to the loan.

faqs.q: Is a longer tenure always cheaper per month?
faqs.a: It lowers the monthly payment but raises total interest. Stretching a 100,000 loan from 10 to 20 years at 9.5% cuts the payment from about 1,294 to 932 but roughly doubles the interest paid.

disclaimer: Estimates use the standard reducing-balance formula and exclude lender fees, insurance and variable-rate changes.
editorial_note: The schedule is the useful part: it shows when prepayment actually pays off, which a single monthly figure cannot.

Stacked coupons, member discounts and sale-on-sale pricing all behave this way.

faqs.q: How do I calculate the original price from a sale price?
faqs.a: Divide the sale price by 1 minus the discount rate. A 60 item at 25% off came from 60 ÷ 0.75 = 80. Adding 25% to 60 instead gives 75, which is wrong — that is the classic reverse-percentage error.

faqs.q: Are two 20% discounts the same as 40% off?
faqs.a: No. Two 20% discounts compound to 36% off, because the second applies to the already discounted price. 100 becomes 80, then 64.

faqs.q: Is a discount applied before or after tax?
faqs.a: In most jurisdictions a trade discount reduces the taxable amount, so tax is calculated on the discounted price. Store coupons usually behave the same way, while manufacturer rebates are often applied after tax has been charged.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a discount and a markup?
faqs.a: A discount reduces a selling price from above; a markup increases a cost price to reach a selling price. A 50% discount requires a 100% markup to return to the original price, which is why heavy discounting is so hard to recover from.

disclaimer: Currency is not converted; enter prices in the currency you are shopping in.
editorial_note: The stacked-discount mode exists because that is where nearly all real shopping mistakes happen.

faqs.q: Should the start date be counted?
faqs.a: It depends on the context. Legal notice periods usually start the day after notice is given, so the start date is excluded. Interest calculations and hotel stays often count nights, not days. This calculator lets you choose, because guessing wrong shifts the answer by a day.

faqs.q: How are working days counted?
faqs.a: Weekdays are Monday to Friday, excluding Saturday and Sunday. Public holidays are not deducted automatically because they differ by country and even by region — check your national holiday calendar if a deadline is critical.

faqs.q: Why does the month total sometimes look odd?
faqs.a: Months have 28 to 31 days, so a month-based duration is an approximation of calendar months. From 31 January, one month later is 28 or 29 February, not 31 February. The years-months-days breakdown avoids this by using real calendar boundaries.

faqs.q: Does this handle leap years?
faqs.a: Yes. 29 February is counted in leap years, so February has 29 days and any span crossing it includes the extra day.

disclaimer: Public holidays and jurisdiction-specific counting rules are not applied automatically.
editorial_note: The inclusive/exclusive toggle is the feature that matters most; most disputes come from that single day.

The complication is the threshold and the base: in the United States federal rules generally require 1.5 times the regular rate above 40 hours in a workweek, while in the UK there is no statutory right to premium overtime pay at all — it depends on your contract.

This calculator takes either an hourly rate or an annual salary, applies the threshold you specify, and supports two different overtime rates in the same week, which covers the common case of weekday overtime at 1.5x and weekend or holiday work at 2x.

faqs.q: What is time and a half?
faqs.a: One and a half times your normal hourly rate. At 20 an hour, overtime is paid at 30. It is the most common premium rate in the United States, the UK and Ireland, though it is a contractual matter in the UK rather than a statutory right.

faqs.q: Is overtime pay taxed more than normal pay?
faqs.a: No. In most countries overtime is taxed as ordinary income, added to your total taxable pay for the period. A bigger payslip in a heavy overtime month can push part of your income into a higher band, which changes the average rate, not a separate overtime tax.

faqs.q: Does overtime start after 8 hours in a day or 40 in a week?
faqs.a: It depends on the jurisdiction. US federal law uses 40 hours in a workweek, though some states add a daily threshold such as California's 8-hour rule. UK law sets no threshold at all. Set the threshold in the calculator to match your applicable rule.

faqs.q: How do I convert my salary to an hourly rate for overtime?
faqs.a: Divide the annual salary by the paid hours the salary covers, typically 2,080 for 40 hours over 52 weeks. A 52,000 salary is 25 an hour, so time and a half is 37.50. Some employers use a different divisor, so check your contract.

faqs.q: Should shift premiums be included in the overtime base?
faqs.a: In the US, the regular rate generally includes non-discretionary payments such as shift differentials, which can raise the overtime rate above the base hourly wage. This calculator uses the rate you enter, so enter the inclusive rate if premiums apply.

disclaimer: Employment law differs by country and state; this is arithmetic, not legal advice on your entitlement.
editorial_note: Two overtime bands are supported because weekend and holiday premiums are where payroll disagreements usually start.

intent_label: Transactional — decided at the table, on a phone, in seconds.
intro: Tipping is a percentage calculation with a cultural variable on top. In the United States 18% to 20% at a sit-down restaurant is customary and often expected; in the UK a discretionary 12.5% service charge is frequently already on the bill; in much of Germany, the Netherlands and Spain rounding up or leaving 5% to 10% is normal; in Japan tipping can be considered impolite.

This calculator handles the arithmetic — tip on the pre-tax or post-tax amount, then an even split between any number of people — and the guide below stops you double-tipping a service charge that is already included.
how_to: Enter the bill amount.
Choose whether the bill already includes tax, and add the tax rate if you want the tip calculated on the pre-tax amount.
Set the tip percentage, or use a preset, then choose how many people are paying.
Read the tip, the total and the per-person share, rounded to a sensible amount.

faqs.q: Should I tip on the pre-tax or post-tax amount?
faqs.a: Most guidance suggests tipping on the pre-tax subtotal, since tax is not part of the service. Many people tip on the total for simplicity; the difference on a typical bill is small. Either way, do not tip on a service charge that is already included.

faqs.q: How much should I tip for delivery?
faqs.a: In the US, 15% to 20% of the order, with a minimum of a few dollars, is common — delivery drivers often rely on tips and may use their own vehicle. In Europe, 5% to 10% or a rounding-up is usually enough.

faqs.q: Is a service charge the same as a tip?
faqs.a: Not always. A mandatory service charge is usually distributed to staff by the employer, sometimes pooled, and in some jurisdictions it is legally treated as part of the employer's revenue. A voluntary tip given directly is more certain to reach the person who served you.

faqs.q: How do I split a bill when people ordered differently?
faqs.a: This tool splits evenly. For uneven bills, calculate each person's share of the food and drink, then apply the same tip percentage to each share — that keeps the tip proportional without needing a separate calculation.

disclaimer: Tipping norms are customary, not legal requirements, and vary by venue and city.
editorial_note: The country table is included because over-tipping on an existing service charge is the most common error we see.

intent_label: Informational — a screening number, usually the start of a deeper question.
intro: Body mass index divides weight in kilograms by height in metres squared. It was designed as a population-level screening tool in the 19th century, and it is still used because it is cheap, reproducible and correlates roughly with body fat across large groups. What it cannot do is tell muscle from fat, which is why a muscular athlete can score as overweight while carrying very little body fat.

This calculator gives your BMI, your category on the World Health Organization adult scale and the weight range that would place you in the healthy band for your height. Read it as a starting point for a conversation, not a diagnosis.
how_to: Choose metric (cm and kg) or imperial (feet, inches and pounds).
Enter your height and weight.

faqs.q: What is a healthy BMI?
faqs.a: The World Health Organization puts the healthy adult range at 18.5 to 24.9. Below 18.5 is underweight, 25 to 29.9 is overweight and 30 or above is obese. The bands are the same for men and women, but not for children.

faqs.q: Is BMI accurate for athletes?
faqs.a: No. BMI cannot distinguish muscle from fat, so strength athletes and rugby players routinely score as overweight or obese while carrying low body fat. Waist-to-height ratio and a body composition measurement are better in that situation.

faqs.q: Does BMI work for children?
faqs.a: Not with adult bands. Children and teenagers need age- and sex-specific percentile charts, because body composition changes rapidly during growth. Ask a paediatrician which chart applies.

faqs.q: Do ethnicity and age change BMI interpretation?
faqs.a: Yes. Some health bodies use lower thresholds for people of South Asian, Chinese, Japanese and other Asian descent, where type 2 diabetes risk rises at a lower BMI. Older adults also carry more fat at the same BMI, so clinicians often combine BMI with waist circumference.

faqs.q: How can I lower my BMI?
faqs.a: Gradual, sustainable changes work better than crash diets: a modest calorie deficit, more protein and fibre, strength training to preserve muscle, and 150 minutes of moderate activity a week. Speak to a doctor before starting a strict plan, especially with existing conditions.

disclaimer: BMI is a screening tool, not a diagnosis, and is not medical advice.
editorial_note: We show the boundaries and the healthy weight range so the number can be interpreted, rather than presented as a verdict.
